title: Yudhishthira's dog
hookLine: at the top of the world, a god offers Yudhishthira heaven on one condition: leave the dog behind
carry: the divine in every creature, even a dog
tomorrow: what does Yudhishthira find when he reaches heaven?

cards: Two of them are left on the mountain: a king and a dog. Yudhishthira's brothers have fallen behind him. Draupadi has fallen.
The dog that joined them at the start of the road is still at his heel. Then the sky fills with sound, and Indra, king of the gods, pulls up in a chariot. Climb in, he says.
Heaven is waiting. This is the moment the whole road has led to. And in Ganguli's telling, Yudhishthira's first answer is not yes.
It's a question about who gets to come with him.

teach.b: First he asks about his brothers and Draupadi; he won't go without them.
Indra reassures him: they left their bodies on the way and are already in heaven. You, he says, will go up in yours. Then Yudhishthira says the dog has been devoted to him, and it should come too.
Indra says no. You have won heaven and a state like a god's. Leave the dog; there is no cruelty in that.
Heaven has no place for people with dogs. Notice how reasonable it sounds. It's only a dog, the offer is enormous, and no one else will speak for it.
Turning away one who is devoted to you, who is frightened and has nowhere else to go, he says, is a grave wrong, and he will not do it even for his own happiness. Then the dog changes.
It is Dharma, the god of righteousness, Yudhishthira's own father, walking beside him in disguise.

Dharma praises him and recalls an earlier test at a forest lake, when Yudhishthira chose to bring back Nakula, son of his father's other wife, out of fairness. Only then does he climb into the chariot. Now the twist.
In the old purity rules a dog counted as unclean, and Indra's words echo that. Yet Dharma himself chose that shape.

teach.h: THE SAME SELF IN EVERY CREATURE
teach.b: The Gita says the wise see the same in a learned priest, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and an outcast. One self, in the king and in the dog.

how: The story of Yudhishthira and the dog comes from the Mahaprasthanika Parva and is retold in recitations of the epic. The Gita's teaching that the wise see the same self in every creature is often quoted alongside it, and in Nepal the second day of Tihar, Kukur Tihar, honors dogs with garlands and a tilak.

o: the god of righteousness, who walked beside him as a dog
the king of the gods, who drives the chariot to heaven
the faithful hound that belonged to the Pandava house

games.q: at heaven's door — tap the pairs.
p: the wise see the same in a dog

s: Indra tells Yudhishthira his brothers are lost
he says they are already in heaven, having left their bodies on the way.
the dog turns out to be Yudhishthira's father
it is Dharma, the god of righteousness, who fathered Yudhishthira.
Hindu tradition has always counted dogs as holy
old purity rules counted dogs unclean, and Indra echoes them; the story's twist is that Dharma chose that shape.

games.q: you're Yudhishthira. a god offers you heaven right now, if you leave behind the dog that has followed you the whole way. what do you do?
o: climb in; it's only a dog.
refuse to go without the dog.
ask the dog to wait for you.
games.why: he refuses to turn away one who is devoted and frightened, and the dog reveals itself as Dharma, his father. the lowliest follower carried the god.

practice: Find one living creature near you: a pet, a bird outside the window, a person across the room. For a minute, just look at it, without naming it useful or annoying, clean or dirty.
As you breathe, think: the same life that's in me is in this one. If you pray, you can see the Lord there; if not, simply see the creature.

wordCard.voice: Dharma. The god of righteousness, who walked beside Yudhishthira the whole way as a dog, and revealed himself only at the gate of heaven.
